description: We're Los Llama Masters 🔥🦙, a team passionate about technology, space, and problem-solving. We're tackling satellite wildfire detection and looking for teammates skilled in programming, data science, GIS, or design. All skill levels are welcome!
summary: Tonalli ATLAS is a free web atlas of NASA FIRMS active-fire hotspots for 235 countries and territories, from November 2000 through the latest days. MODIS and VIIRS cannot be joined raw. MODIS sees roughly 1 km pixels from 2000. VIIRS sees 375 m pixels from 2012 and reports several times more hotspots for the same burns, so a raw time series jumps in 2012. We put every month on the VIIRS NOAA-20 scale: one real VIIRS satellite from 2012 on, and before that a MODIS count converted with a ratio per 0.5° cell and a factor per calendar month, tested by leaving one year out. At tonalli.earth/atlas you pick a country or draw an area and get the calendar the challenge asks for: the fire season, years above or below the usual level, this month against its median, and the last 7 days by sensor. The map plays month by month, colored by hotspot count or by brightness temperature, with Harmonized, MODIS-only and VIIRS-only views, and every series downloads as CSV. A hotspot is a hot pixel, not a fire and not burned area.
details:
What it does

Tonalli ATLAS (tonalli.earth/atlas) is a read-only map of NASA FIRMS hotspots. You choose one of 235 countries and territories, combine several, or draw your own area: a rectangle, a free shape, or a box typed in from coordinates. For that area you get a calendar that starts in November 2000. It shows the three-month fire season, which years sit above or below a usual year, how the month so far compares with its average, and where the latest complete month falls in its usual range. The last 7 days appear as individual points. Each one keeps its satellite, confidence, fire radiative power and brightness temperature, and the map can show MODIS, VIIRS, or both.

The same map plays the monthly history. Cells are colored by hotspot count or by brightness temperature in °C, °F or K. You can switch between three records: Harmonized, MODIS only and VIIRS only. The monthly series and the 7-day points download as CSV.

How it works

Jobs on Railway pull the FIRMS yearly country archives and the near-real-time area API into Cloudflare R2 as Parquet. The world archive is on the order of 50 GB of CSV, so that work stays in the cloud. A second stage removes static heat sources (gas flares, volcanoes, industry) and low-confidence hotspots (MODIS under 30, VIIRS low). It then assigns each point to a country and a state using geoBoundaries and counts hotspots per satellite, per 0.1° cell and per month, with a mean brightness temperature.

Harmonization is needed because the two sensors don't count the same way. In Brazil, one MODIS hotspot is about 3.7 VIIRS hotspots for the same fires, and the site shows each country's own ratio. It happens in the export, on the VIIRS NOAA-20 scale, since VIIRS is the sensor still flying. From 2012 on, each month comes from one satellite: NOAA-20, or NOAA-21 scaled to it, or S-NPP scaled to it. Satellites are never added together. From November 2000 through early 2012, the VIIRS-equivalent count is MODIS times a ratio per 0.5° cell, a factor per calendar month, and a Terra-only correction for the years before Aqua. Cell ratios shrink toward the country ratio, and small countries can borrow the world ratio. To score it, we hide one year at a time and compare the estimate with real VIIRS on error, bias, and whether the years still rank in the same order. If the cell model doesn't beat a simpler ratio, that country or state keeps the simpler one. Reconstructed months carry a p10 to p90 band.

Those exports are small JSON files. A Cloudflare Worker written with Hono only reads them, and the same Worker serves the landing page and the atlas. Opening a country doesn't trigger any calculation, and versioned files stay cached at the edge for a year.

On the harmonized temperature view, MODIS brightness is quantile-mapped in the browser onto the VIIRS I4 scale, using the cell-months both sensors observed. That value is for the whole pixel, roughly 36 to 75 °C, not the flame itself. VIIRS I4 saturates near 367 K.

Benefits

You can put 2005 next to 2024 and trust the comparison, because both are on the same scale. A high year isn't just an artifact of the sensor change in 2012. MODIS and VIIRS stay one click away, and a chart plots converted MODIS against real VIIRS from 2012 onward so anyone can check the join. There's no account. A drawn area gets the same calendar as a whole country. The CSVs keep each month's status (missing, partial or provisional) along with the harmonized count and the raw MODIS count.

Intended impact

A land manager or a researcher should be able to open their country and see the season, the unusual years and this month without first learning two satellite products. We've written a forecasting plan that compares a seasonal baseline with gradient boosting and TimeGPT, but no model has been trained and the live tool doesn't predict anything. Six volunteers in El Salvador built it on public NASA data. The terms say it isn't for evacuation or any life-safety decision. The latest days are provisional, and the years before 2012 are an estimate.

How it is creative

The screen is a calendar: twelve months, a year you can play across the map, and the same questions whether you pick a country or a shape you drew. The detailed correction is allowed to lose. Where a per-cell ratio doesn't beat one national ratio on held-out years, we publish the simpler number and say so. The correction can also be turned off. Temperature gets its own harmonization, fitted in the browser, so the color ramp doesn't jump when the sensor changes.

What we considered

  • A hotspot is one hot pixel, and one fire makes many of them. We don't report burned area.
  • A month with no data stays blank, and a real zero stays zero. Partial months stay out of averages and ranks.
  • Two satellites are never added in the same month, because that would count the same fire twice.
  • NOAA-20 is the common scale because that series continues.
  • The record before 2012 is a reconstruction with an uncertainty band.
  • Near-real-time days are marked provisional, and the last 7 days aren't written into the monthly history.
  • The sites need no account, work on a phone and respect reduced motion.

Tools, languages, hardware, software

Development

Git and GitHub, mise for tool versions, uv for Python and Bun 1.4.4. Vite+ (Vite, Oxlint, Oxfmt), Ruff and basedpyright. The API is tested with bun test and the landing page with Vitest. The atlas is checked by hand in the browser.

Hosting

One Cloudflare Worker serves the API and both sites, deployed with Wrangler. All data lives in R2. Railway runs the Docker jobs: 4 extract workers, a prepare step, 8 processing shards and an export. The domain is tonalli.earth.

API

Hono in TypeScript, read-only. Routes: /healthz, /v1/places, and one file per place (meta, monthly, grid, recent, outline).

Web

React 18, TypeScript and Tailwind CSS v4. MapLibre GL for the globe, terra-draw for drawn areas, d3 scales for the SVG charts, vaul for the phone drawer, papaparse for CSV and motion for animation. The landing globe is a canvas drawn with d3-geo. Typeface: Public Sans.

Languages.

Python 3.12, TypeScript, SQL in DuckDB, HTML and CSS.

Data and geospatial

DuckDB over Parquet, NumPy, shapely, pandas and GeoPandas. Grids at 0.1° and 0.5°. Borders from geoBoundaries CGAZ ADM1. Basemaps from NASA GIBS (Blue Marble, and VIIRS night lights from 2016). Map style from OpenFreeMap. Land outlines from Natural Earth, through world-atlas.

Caching

Versioned JSON is cached as immutable for a year, and the place list refreshes every 60 seconds. A new export changes the version hash, so the site picks it up within a minute.

HardwareOur own laptops and desktop PCs. The heavy processing ran on Railway and Cloudflare.Data sources

NASA FIRMS active-fire hotspots: MODIS on Terra and Aqua, VIIRS on S-NPP, NOAA-20 and NOAA-21, from the yearly country archives and the near-real-time area API. State borders from geoBoundaries CGAZ ADM1. Basemap imagery from NASA GIBS.

Use of AI

We used Devin, Claude Code, Cursor and Codex CLI as coding assistants to write and review the websites and the API. The sun icon was made in pen.dev with Codex CLI. The repo includes an AGENTS.md file so those tools follow the same data rules we do. None of the figures on the site come from a generative model. Harmonization is a documented statistical correction, checked against VIIRS years that were left out of the fit. The team chose the method, the validation and the wording of the limits.
